blocks.content: A Kubernetes Event is a record of something that happened to an object, generated automatically by whichever component was involved, often the fastest way to learn exactly why something went wrong.
1. A Record of Something That Happened
blocks.text: 1. A Record of Something That Happened

blocks.content: Events are not something you create yourself, they are automatically generated records, "this Pod was scheduled," "this image pull failed," "this probe check failed," a running log of notable occurrences tied to a specific object.

blocks.alt: Automatically generated, a running log of notable occurrences, not something you author

blocks.content: Any part of the cluster can generate an Event, the scheduler (a placement decision or failure), kubelet (a probe result, an image pull), or a controller (a scaling decision), covered throughout the Architecture module, whichever component actually did something notable.

blocks.alt: Any component in the cluster can be the source of a given Event

blocks.content: Beyond the Events attached to one specific object via describe, covered in the previous topic, kubectl get events shows every recent Event across a namespace, or the whole cluster, useful for getting a broader picture of what has been happening recently.

blocks.alt: The full picture, not scoped to just one specific object

blocks.content: This is a genuine, practical limitation worth knowing, Events have a limited retention window (commonly around an hour by default), if you are investigating something that happened a while ago, the relevant Events may already be gone.

blocks.alt: A real limitation, worth checking sooner rather than later after something goes wrong

blocks.content: 5. Often the Fastest Way to Learn Why
blocks.text: 5. Often the Fastest Way to Learn Why

blocks.content: A message like FailedScheduling: Insufficient memory tells you, immediately and precisely, exactly why a Pod is stuck Pending, covered in the Pod Phases topic, no guessing, no piecing together clues from elsewhere required.

blocks.alt: A precise, direct answer, often faster than any other debugging approach

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: Events are automatically generated records of notable occurrences, from any cluster component, and kubectl get events shows the full recent picture, not just one object's.
They have a limited retention window, worth checking promptly, and are very often the fastest, most direct way to learn exactly why something went wrong.
